summary: This unit teaches you to run a guest laundry service in a villa, guest house or hotel: collect and check the laundry, read care labels and sort, pre-treat stains, wash and dry correctly, iron, fold and package, and return the order and charge it. You will also learn to handle soiled linen hygienically, use chemicals and machines safely, and look after linen stock.

blocks.p: Guests judge a property by small things, and clean, well-pressed clothes returned on time and complete are one of them. This unit covers the whole laundry service, from the moment you collect the guest's bag to the moment you hand the order back and put the charge on the bill. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

A laundry worker holds a guest's property. A shirt shrunk by the wrong wash, a dark dress that runs onto white sheets, a phone washed in a pocket or a missing item can cost the property money and a guest's trust. That is why this unit is about **checking, reading labels and following the rules** as much as it is about washing and ironing.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's laundry and mock villa. In the practical tasks the assessor sets small tests in the bag, such as a count that does not match the list or an item in a pocket. The assessor watches your checking, reporting and safety, not only the finished clothes.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Take photographs of the work and the laundry only. Do not photograph a real guest's belongings, names or room numbers.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A laundry has heat, steam, water, electricity, moving machinery and chemicals in one room. Most injuries are slips, burns, strain from lifting wet loads, and chemical splashes. Most fires start in dryers and irons. Learn the hazards before you switch anything on.

blocks.h: Hazards and how you prevent them

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Wet floor, spilled water or detergent powder
Slips and falls; powder is very slippery when wet
Wipe up at once
Put out a wet floor sign until the floor is dry
Do not wash spilt powder into the drain with strong chemicals
Hot iron, steam and hot machines
Burns and scalds
Stand the iron upright or switch it off and unplug it when you leave the board
Keep cables off the hot plate and out of walkways
Keep your hands clear of steam
Never open a machine door while the drum is turning
Flatwork ironer (roller ironer)
Hands, fingers or hair pulled between the hot rollers
Use it only if you are trained
Tie back long hair; no loose sleeves or jewellery
Feed sheets from the correct side with your hands well back
Know where the emergency stop is
Tumble dryer and lint
Fire
Clean the lint filter after every load
Never overload; do not pile up warm laundry
Keep the area around the dryer clear
Chemicals: detergent, bleach, stain remover
Burns to skin and eyes; poisonous fumes when mixed
Read the label and the safety data sheet
Wear gloves and eye protection when measuring or pouring
Never mix products
Keep each in its own labelled container
Lifting wet linen
Back strain; wet sheets are very heavy
Take a little out at a time into a trolley
Bend your knees, keep your back straight
Do not lean into a deep drum with your legs straight
Electrical equipment near water
Shock; fire
Dry your hands before touching switches and plugs
Report damaged cables and plugs; do not use the item
Hot, humid air
Heat exhaustion
Drink water; take breaks as the property allows
Keep fans and windows working

ul: A **safety data sheet (SDS)** comes with every chemical product. It tells you the hazards, how to use it safely, what protective clothing to wear, first aid and how to deal with a spill. Know where the SDS file is kept.
The **label** tells you how much to use and what the warning symbols mean. Follow it exactly.
Never mix chemicals. **Chlorine bleach mixed with an ammonia cleaner, or with an acid cleaner, gives off a poisonous gas.** If this happens, leave the room, open the doors and call your supervisor.
Never pour a product into an unlabelled bottle or a drinks bottle.
Store products in a cool, dry, locked place, off the floor and away from heat and sunlight.

blocks.note: If liquid detergent or bleach splashes in your eye, **rinse it at once with plenty of clean running water** for several minutes, keeping the eye open, and get help. Do not rub the eye, and do not put anything else in it. Tell your supervisor and write it in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Jamaica uses 110 V (and 220 V for some heavy machines) at 50 Hz. Make sure a machine is rated for the socket it is plugged into. Water cuts happen in dry spells, so know what to do if the water stops with a load in the machine, and ask your supervisor before you open the door of a full drum.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Wash your hands before and after handling dirty linen and after using chemicals. Cover cuts with a waterproof plaster.
Wear gloves for dirty linen and chemicals, and non-slip closed shoes.
Keep clean linen away from your uniform and your body; do not put clean items on the floor.
Report sore skin early: wet work and detergents can cause dermatitis.

blocks.p: The laundry list is the agreement between the guest and the property. It says what was sent, what service was wanted and what it will cost. Every later check depends on it.

head: What the list shows
Why it matters
rows: Guest's name and room or villa number
So the order goes back to the right person.
Date and time collected
So you can meet the promised return time.
Each item and how many
The count in the laundry is checked against it.
Service wanted: normal or express (a faster service at an extra charge)
Sets the return time and the price.
Special instructions, for example hand wash, starch or hanger
Tells you how to treat the order.
Price for each item and the total
Goes on the guest's bill.
Signature or initials of the guest and the staff member
Proves what was handed over.

blocks.h: Collecting and checking, step by step

flow: Collect the bag from the room or the guest at the time the property says
Check that the list is filled in: name, room number, service and items
Take the bag to the laundry and count every item against the list
Record any difference on the list
Empty every pocket; set aside what you find
Look over each item for stains, tears, missing buttons and faded colour
Note all damage on the list
Tell the guest or supervisor about any problem before washing
Tag the order with the room number so it stays together

head: What you find
What you do
rows: Fewer items than the list
Do not change the guest's list. Write the count you found beside it, and tell the guest or supervisor before washing. Look again in the bag and in the room.
More items than the list
Write them on the list as 'found, not listed', and tell the guest or supervisor. Do not wash or charge for them until it is agreed.
An item the list does not describe correctly, for example 'shirt' for a dress
Note it and ask the guest or supervisor.
Items that look like several guests' laundry
Keep each guest's order apart and tagged.

blocks.note: Never wash an item you suspect is wrong, damaged or not the guest's, and never alter the guest's list. Writing your own note beside it keeps the record honest and protects both the guest and you.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Check **every pocket** of every item, including swimwear, beach bags and jackets. Pens leak and spoil a whole load, tissues shred into lint, sand and shells wear out machines, and coins, keys and phones can break the drum or be ruined.

Money, jewellery, phones, cards, keys and papers are the guest's property. Do not keep them, read them or move them. Record what you found and where, put it in a safe place, and return it by the property's rules, usually through the supervisor or front desk, with a note on the list.
Foreign money, such as a US$ note, is returned in the same way: it is never kept as a tip.
Look at collars, cuffs, underarms, seams, hems, buttons, zips and the care label.
Note stains (what colour, where, how big), rips, holes, loose buttons, missing buttons, faded patches and burn marks.
Write what you see in plain words on the list. Tell the guest before you wash if the item may not survive the wash, for example a very old, thin or heavily stained garment.
If a label says dry clean only, tell the guest or supervisor. The property may send it to a dry cleaner, or decline it.

blocks.note: If a guest asks for a quick return on the same day, tell them honestly whether the express service can meet the time. Promising and then failing is worse than saying no at the start.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Common fibres and how they behave

head: Fibre
Where you meet it
Washing and drying
Ironing
rows: Cotton
Sheets, towels, shirts, shorts, T-shirts
Takes hot water and strong washing. Shrinks and creases if over-dried.
Hot (highest setting); damp helps
Linen (from flax)
Resort shirts, trousers, table linen
Washes well; creases very easily.
Hot, while still damp
Polyester, nylon, acrylic (man-made)
Sports wear, swimwear, blouses, curtains
Cooler wash; dries quickly. Too much heat melts or shrinks it.
Cool or warm only
Wool
Jumpers, cardigans, suits
Shrinks and felts (goes thick and hard) in hot water and rough washing. Hand wash or a wool programme, dry flat.
Warm, with a cloth or steam
Silk
Blouses, scarves, ties
Delicate; gentle wash by hand or dry clean. Colour often runs.
Cool, inside out, with a cloth
Blends (for example cotton and polyester)
Many shirts and uniforms
Wash and iron by the more delicate fibre.
Follow the label

blocks.p: A **care label** is sewn into the item. Its symbols are the maker's instructions. Look at the label on every item. There are five main groups of symbols: the washtub, the triangle, the square, the iron and the circle.

head: Symbol
What it shows
What the signs mean
rows: Washtub
Washing
A number: the highest water temperature in degrees Celsius, for example 40 means wash at no more than 40 °C
Dots may be used instead of numbers: more dots, hotter
A hand in the tub: hand wash only
Bars under the tub: use a gentler cycle (one bar gentle, two bars very gentle)
Crossed tub: do not wash
Triangle
Bleaching
Empty triangle: any bleach may be used
Triangle with two slanted lines: non-chlorine (oxygen) bleach only
Crossed triangle: do not bleach
Square
Drying
Square with a circle inside: tumble drying allowed; dots show the heat (one dot lower, two dots normal)
Crossed square and circle: do not tumble dry
Lines inside the square show line drying, drip drying, drying flat or drying in the shade
Iron
Ironing
One dot: cool (about 110 °C)
Two dots: warm (about 150 °C)
Three dots: hot (about 200 °C)
Crossed iron: do not iron; crossed steam lines: do not steam
Circle
Professional cleaning
Plain circle: dry cleaning
Letters inside tell the dry cleaner which solvent to use
Crossed circle: do not dry clean

blocks.note: Symbols are the same in many countries, but the number of dots and the exact wording can differ a little between makers. If a label is missing, faded or unclear, treat the item as delicate: cool wash, no bleach, no tumble drying, and ask your supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Sorting makes sure every item gets the wash it needs and nothing is spoiled. Sort in this order, and do it before anything goes into a machine.

flow: Keep each guest's order together and tagged
Read the care label on every item
Separate by colour: whites, light colours, darks, and new or bright items
Separate by fabric and care: hot-wash cottons, cooler synthetics, delicates, wool and silk
Separate by how dirty: heavily soiled items apart from light ones
Set aside stained items for pre-treatment
Set aside dry-clean-only items and ask the supervisor

head: Sort by
Why
Example
rows: Colour
Dye can run and stain lighter items.
New dark red beach towels are washed alone the first time, not with white sheets.
Fabric and care label
Different fabrics need different heat and treatment.
White cotton pillowcases go with white cotton sheets; a wool jumper does not.
How dirty
Heavy soil and grease can pass to clean items.
Dirty pool towels are washed apart from guest shirts.
Guest
Prevents mixing up items or losing them.
Mesh bags and tags keep one guest's socks and swimwear together.

ul: Wash delicate items such as lace, bras and swimwear in a **mesh wash bag**. It stops them stretching and tangling.
Close zips, hooks and Velcro, and turn dark items inside out to protect the colour.
If you are not sure whether a colour will run, wet a hidden corner, press it on a white cloth, and see whether colour comes off. If it does, wash it alone.

blocks.note: On a sorting sheet, write each pile and why: for example 'whites, cotton, 60 °C' or 'dark, cool, inside out'. The assessor and your supervisor can then see your thinking.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A stain is easiest to remove when it is fresh and has not met heat. **Pre-treating** means treating a stain before the item goes into the wash. Any stain left by washing and then dried is much harder to remove.

ul: Treat stains **early**: a fresh stain comes out far more easily than an old one.
**Never dry or iron an item that still has a stain.** Heat from the dryer or the iron **sets** the stain: it becomes fixed in the fabric and will not come out.
**Test** any stain remover on a hidden part first. Some remove colour or damage the fabric.
Blot, do not rub: rubbing spreads the stain and damages the fibres.
Work from the outside of the stain towards the middle so it does not spread.
Check the care label and use only a product that suits that fabric.
Wear gloves and never mix stain products.

head: Stain
What kind
What to do before the wash
rows: Blood, egg, milk, sweat
Protein: heat cooks it into the fabric
Rinse or soak in **cold** water first, never hot. Then a suitable pre-treater or enzyme product and wash.
Oil, sunscreen, butter, make-up
Grease
Blot, then a suitable grease remover or liquid detergent worked in. Wash at the hottest temperature the label allows.
Curry, tomato sauce, jerk sauce, sorrel, red wine
Strong colour
Remove the lumps, rinse with cold water from the back, then use a stain remover that suits the fabric. Some of the colour may stay.
Grass, mud
Dirt and plant
Let mud dry and brush it off, then pre-treat and wash.
Ink, felt-tip pen
Dye
Blot gently, use a remover made for ink if the label allows, and test it first. Do not rub.
Rust
Iron stain
Use a rust remover made for textiles, following the maker, on fabrics it suits. Chlorine bleach makes rust worse.
Deodorant, perfume, tea, coffee
Mixed
Pre-treat with a stain remover and wash as the label allows.

blocks.note: Do not rub salt, lime or other kitchen products into a guest's clothes. They can spoil dyes and fabrics, and they will not do the work of a proper stain remover. If a stain will not come out after treatment, tell the guest or supervisor; do not keep washing and drying it.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Find the stain and note it on the list
Read the care label
Choose a suitable stain remover and read its label
Test it on a hidden part
Apply to the stain and leave it for the time on the label
Rinse or wash as the product says
Check that the stain has gone before drying
If it has not, repeat or report; do not dry it

blocks.p: Stains from guests often include sunscreen on white and pastel items, food and drink at villa dinners, and sand and mud from the beach. Treat them while you sort; do not let them wait in the basket.

blocks.note: If a stain is on white cotton only, an oxygen bleach (non-chlorine) is usually safe and works well. Chlorine bleach can destroy colours, wool and silk and turn some stains yellow.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A wash has four jobs: loosen the dirt, hold it in the water, rinse it away and spin out the water. The result depends on four things: **water, detergent, heat and movement** (and the time they work). Too little of one and the wash is poor; too much and the fabric is damaged.

ul: Check the drum for items left from the last wash, and check the filters and dispensers are clear.
Check that sorting and pre-treatment are done and that pockets are empty.
Check that the water and power are on and the door seals are clean.

head: Point
What to do
Why
rows: Load size
Load only to the capacity the maker gives (often a weight in kg), not packed tight and not a single item.
Items must move freely to get clean and rinse. Overloading wears the machine and leaves dirt; a very small load wastes water and power.
Detergent
Measure it using the label for the load size, how dirty the load is and the water hardness. Use the dispenser or dosing system.
Too little leaves dirt; too much leaves residue, makes towels stiff and is hard to rinse out.
Heat
Choose the temperature by the care label and the most delicate item in the load.
Hot water cleans and disinfects better; the wrong temperature shrinks, fades or melts fabric.
Programme
Choose by fabric and soil: for example cotton hot, synthetics cooler, delicates gentle, wool special.
The cycle sets the temperature, movement and time.

ul: **Chlorine bleach** whitens and disinfects but is strong. Use it only where the care label allows, usually on white cotton, in its own dispenser or as the maker says. Never put it on wool, silk or coloured items and never mix it with other products.
**Oxygen (non-chlorine) bleach** is milder and is usually safer for coloured fabrics.
**Fabric softener** is added in the **rinse**, never with the detergent. It makes items feel soft and cuts static, but it can make towels less absorbent, so use it as the property says.
Use the property's products, as the maker says. Do not mix products from different bottles.

flow: Pre-wash for very dirty items, if the programme has one
Main wash with detergent, heat and movement
Rinses until the water is clear
Softener in the final rinse, if used
Spin or extraction to remove the water

blocks.p: A **washer-extractor** is a machine that washes and then spins the load at speed. A separate **hydro-extractor** spins water out of a washed load before drying. Never open a door while the drum is still turning.

head: Load
Typical temperature
Notes
rows: White cotton sheets, pillowcases, towels
60 °C or hotter, as the label allows
Hot water and detergent clean and help kill germs.
Coloured cotton
Check for colour running.
Synthetics
Too hot and they crease, shrink or melt.
Wool and silk
Cold or 30 °C, gentle or by hand
Hot water and rough washing shrink and felt wool.
Soiled or infected linen
As the property's rule says, often 65 °C or hotter for at least 10 minutes
Follow the written procedure.

blocks.note: These are guides. Always use the care label, the machine maker's instructions and the property's rules. If the load has a delicate item, the whole load goes on the more delicate setting, or the item is washed alone.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Unload promptly. Wet laundry left in the drum or in a basket can smell of mildew and creases badly.
Take wet loads out a little at a time into a trolley, bending your knees.
Check every item: is the stain gone, is the colour right, is anything torn? If a stain remains, treat it again before drying.
Shake out each item so it dries well and creases less.

head: Problem
Likely cause
Cure or prevention
rows: White items turned pink or grey
A coloured item ran, or a mixed load
Sort more carefully; wash new coloured items alone first
Wool shrunk and felted
Hot water or rough washing
Wash by the label; cool and gentle; dry flat
Towels stiff or not absorbent
Too much detergent or softener
Measure carefully and rinse well
Grey dull whites
Too little detergent, low heat, overloading
Load to capacity; use enough detergent and the right heat
Stain still there
Not pre-treated, or dried first
Pre-treat; never dry a stained item
Sour or musty smell
Left damp too long
Unload promptly and dry fully

head: Method
Good for
Take care
rows: Tumble drying
Towels, sheets, cotton items that the label allows
Over-drying shrinks, creases and wears cotton. Clean the filter after every load. Use a lower heat for synthetics.
Line drying
Sheets, shirts, most items on a sunny day
Strong sun fades dark colours, and drying outdoors can make items stiff. Dry dark items inside out and in the shade.
Drying flat
Wool, swimwear, stretchy and knitted items
Hanging heavy wet items stretches them. Lay them on a clean, dry towel in the shade.
Drip drying
Items that crease easily
Hang them wet without wringing.

blocks.note: Jamaican sun dries clothes fast but fades dark items and weakens elastic. Dry dark clothes inside out and out of strong sun. Stretchy fabrics, such as swimsuits, dry better flat or on a line in the shade, not in strong sun by the pool.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Clean the lint filter and check the dryer is empty
Check that items are suitable and not still stained
Shake out wet items and load loosely, not above the maker's capacity
Select the heat and time for the lightest fabric
Close the door and start the dryer
At the end let it cool down, then unload at once and fold or hang
Clean the lint filter again

ul: **Lint** is the fluffy fibre that comes off cloth. It collects in the filter. A full filter slows drying, makes the dryer overheat and can catch fire, so clean it after **every** load.
Check the vent pipe and the area around the dryer. Keep them free of lint and dust.
Never overload: items need room to tumble and dry.
Never dry items that have been soaked in oil, petrol, cooking oil or other flammable substances.
If a dryer smells of burning, makes a strange noise or gets very hot, switch it off and report it. Do not open the door until you are sure there is no fire.

blocks.note: Linen soaked in oil, such as massage towels from a spa, can heat up by itself and catch fire, even after leaving the dryer. Wash it well, use the cool-down part of the cycle, and do not leave it piled up warm. Follow the property's procedure.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Items should be completely dry. Damp items grow mildew and smell.
Cotton items left in a hot dryer too long shrink, crease badly and wear out faster. Take them out while slightly damp if they are to be ironed.
Fold or hang items promptly so they do not crease.
Check that the board is stable and the cover is clean, and the iron and cable are undamaged.
Read the care label. If the fabric is unknown, **test the heat on a hidden part** first.
Use a **pressing cloth**, a thin cloth between the iron and the fabric, for silk, dark fabrics, wool and anything that may shine.
Fill a steam iron with water only when it is **unplugged**, as the maker says. Use the type of water the maker recommends.
Sort the ironing by heat: do the **lowest-heat** items first, then work up. The iron cools slowly, so it is easier to wait for it to warm than to cool.

head: Fabric
Heat
Notes
rows: Synthetics (polyester, nylon, acrylic)
Cool: one dot
Easy to melt or shine.
Silk, wool
Cool to warm; press cloth
Iron silk inside out; steam wool with a cloth.
Cotton
Hot: three dots
Damp helps remove creases.
Linen
Hot, while damp
Creases easily; iron on the wrong side first for a shine-free finish.
Dark items
As the fabric allows, inside out
Ironing on the right side can leave a shiny mark.

flow: Test the heat and set it for the fabric
Collar: the underside first, then the top
Cuffs: inside first, then outside
Sleeves: lay flat, iron both sides from the seam
Yoke (the shoulder panel): over the narrow end of the board
Back: lay flat and iron
Front panels and button strip, going round the buttons
Hang it on a hanger, or button and fold it

blocks.p: The order works from the small, hard parts to the large flat ones, so the bigger areas are not creased again while you handle the small ones.

ul: Move the iron smoothly in long strokes. Do not leave it still on one place.
Iron a dark item **inside out** so the iron does not leave a shine.
A **crease** in trousers is pressed along the leg seam with a pressing cloth, using steam for wool blends. Lay the legs flat and match the seams.
If the item still has a stain, do not iron it: heat sets it. Treat it again.

blocks.note: When you leave the board, even for a moment, **stand the iron upright or switch it off and unplug it**. Never leave it face down, or lay it on clothes or let the cable hang over the edge. Keep the cable off the hot plate and out of walkways.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Shine marks, scorching and other problems

head: Problem
Cause
Prevention
rows: Shiny patch
Iron too hot, or ironing dark fabric on the right side
Iron inside out or use a pressing cloth
Scorch mark
Heat too high or iron left still
Test the heat; keep the iron moving
Melted fabric
Synthetic ironed too hot
Check the label; use cool
New creases
Folding before the item is cool or dry
Let the item cool, then fold
Water spots
Spitting steam iron
Use the right water; let the iron heat up

ul: Fold the same way every time. Towels and sheets stack neatly, fit the shelves and look the same.
Shirts are returned buttoned and folded or on hangers, as the guest asked; trousers on hangers with the crease, or folded; socks and underwear in a neat pile.
Use tissue or a shirt bag for items that crease easily. Keep each guest's order together.
Pack clean items only into a clean bag or box, and attach the list and the room number.

sections.title: Returning orders, charges, complaints and linen stock

flow: Check every item on the list is there and clean
Check for creases, stains and missing buttons
Package the order and attach the room number
Work out the charge on the list
Deliver at the agreed time; knock and announce
Hand over the order and explain it
Add the charge to the room bill and file the list

ul: If an item is not ready or a stain remains, tell the guest honestly. Offer to treat it again or explain the problem.
If the guest is not in, **do what the property's rules say**, for example leave it with the front desk or return later. Do not leave it in the corridor or hand it to someone else.
A guest is usually charged by adding the laundry charge on the list to the room bill. You do not take money from the guest at the door.

blocks.p: Multiply the number of each item by its price, then add the lines. Add any express charge. Tax and service charge are added by the property at the current rates; the list may show the total before tax.

head: Item
Number
Price (J$)
Line total (J$)
rows: Shirts
Shorts
Dress
**Total before tax**
8 items

blocks.note: Check the charge twice. A wrong figure on the bill is a complaint waiting to happen.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Missing or damaged items and complaints

flow: Listen calmly and thank the guest for telling you
Check the laundry list and the damage you noted
Search the laundry, the guest's room and the linen areas
Tell your supervisor at once
Follow the property's policy for lost or damaged items
Keep the guest informed and record what happened

ul: Do not blame the guest, argue or promise to pay. The supervisor decides what the property will do.
Your notes on the list, made when you collected and checked the laundry, show whether damage was already there.
Wear gloves and, where needed, an apron. Roll the dirty linen **in on itself**, carry it **away from your body** and do not shake it out: shaking spreads dust and germs.
Put it straight into a laundry bag or bin. Never put dirty linen on the clean linen shelf or on a bed.
Linen with **blood, vomit, faeces or other body fluids** goes into a marked bag and is washed by the property's rule, usually at a high temperature with disinfection.
Keep **clean and dirty linen apart** at all times, with separate trolleys, rooms or areas. Germs from dirty linen must not pass to clean linen.
Wash your hands after handling soiled linen, before touching clean linen and before breaks.

blocks.p: The property keeps enough linen so the rooms are never short while some is being washed. This is controlled using **par levels**. A **par** is the number of sets needed for each bed or room.

head: Term
What it means
rows: Par level of 3
Three sets for each bed: one in use on the bed, one in the wash and one clean on the shelf.
Stock-take
Counting all linen and comparing the count with the records.
Reject
Linen that is stained beyond cleaning, torn or worn out. It is set aside, recorded and not put back in use.
Rotation
Using the oldest clean linen first so all of it wears evenly.

ul: A sheet with a stain that will not come out or with a hole is **set aside as a reject and recorded**. It is not used for a guest, even for one night, and it is not washed again and again.
Rejects may be repaired or turned into cleaning cloths, as the property decides.

blocks.h: At the end of the shift

flow: Switch off and unplug irons
Clean lint filters and dryer vents
Wipe machines and leave doors open to air
Empty and clean the machine dispensers
Return chemicals to the locked store
Sweep and dry the floor
Report faults and low stock, and complete your records

ul: I can name the hazards in a laundry and say how to prevent slips, burns, fires, chemical injuries and back strain.
I can explain why chemicals must never be mixed, and what to do if one gets in an eye.
I can collect a laundry bag, check the list, count the items and record differences.
I can check pockets and deal correctly with money and other items found.
I can note damage on the list and tell the guest or supervisor before washing.
I can read the washtub, triangle, square, iron and circle symbols on a care label.
I can sort laundry by colour, fabric, care and how dirty it is, and use a mesh bag for delicates.
I can pre-treat common stains, test a stain remover and explain why heat sets a stain.
I can load a washer to capacity, measure detergent and choose a programme.
I can say when bleach and fabric softener may and may not be used.
I can dry items safely and prevent lint fires.
I can set the right iron heat and iron a shirt in order.
I can fold and package an order and work out the charge.
I can deal with a missing or damaged item calmly and correctly.
I can handle soiled linen, keep clean and dirty linen apart and reject worn linen.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I check the pockets before washing because pens and coins can ruin the load and the guest's property could be lost.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Laundry list
The form listing the guest's items, the service wanted and the price.
Express service
A faster laundry service at an extra charge.
Care label
The label sewn into clothes showing how to wash, dry and iron them.
Washtub symbol
The care symbol for washing; a number shows the highest temperature.
Mesh wash bag
A net bag that protects delicate items in the wash.
Pre-treating
Treating a stain before the item is washed.
Set (a stain)
Fixed in the fabric, often by heat, so it cannot be removed.
Protein stain
A stain such as blood or egg that heat cooks into the fabric.
Chlorine bleach
A strong bleach for white cotton only where the label allows.
Oxygen bleach
A milder, non-chlorine bleach, safer for colours.
Fabric softener
A product added in the rinse that makes fabric soft.
Washer-extractor
A machine that washes and spins the load.
Lint
Fluffy fibres that collect in a dryer filter and can cause fire.
Pressing cloth
A thin cloth between the iron and the fabric to prevent shine.
Flatwork ironer
A large roller ironer for sheets and tablecloths.
SDS
Safety data sheet: the safety information that comes with a chemical.
Par level
The number of sets of linen held for each bed or room.
Reject
Linen too stained or worn to use, set aside and recorded.
Contaminated linen
Linen soiled with blood or other body fluids.
Cross-contamination
Germs passing from dirty to clean linen.

c1.title: A guest bag at a Negril villa
c1.text: Mr. Anthony Pinnock, a guest at a villa in Negril, leaves a laundry bag for express service. His list shows 2 polo shirts, 1 pair of shorts and 1 swimsuit. When trainee Shanice empties the bag in the laundry, she finds the 2 polo shirts, the shorts, the swimsuit and also a pair of white socks that are not on the list. In the shorts pocket are J$300 in notes and a folded paper with a phone number. One polo shirt has a button missing at the collar. Mr. Pinnock is out on a fishing trip until evening.

c2.title: Sorting at the Centre's laundry
c2.text: In the Centre's laundry in Kingston, trainees Kemar and Alecia are given a mixed basket. It holds white cotton sheets labelled 60 °C, new navy beach towels, a polyester T-shirt labelled 30 °C with the dots symbol on the iron, a lace blouse, a woollen cardigan with a hand in the washtub, and a white napkin with a red sorrel stain. Several items have a crossed circle inside a square.

c3.title: Sunscreen and sauce at an Ocho Rios guest house
c3.text: A guest house in Ocho Rios gets a bag of laundry after a family beach day. It includes white cotton beach towels with oily sunscreen marks, a cream linen shirt with a jerk sauce stain, and a white T-shirt with a stain that the trainee, Dwayne, is not sure about. The labels allow a 60 °C wash on the towels. Dwayne has a spray stain remover that he has not used before.

c4.title: A slow dryer in Montego Bay
c4.text: At a Montego Bay hotel laundry, trainee Natalie notices that a tumble dryer is taking much longer than usual to dry a load, and the outside of the machine feels very hot. The lint filter, which she did not clean after the last load, is covered in thick grey fluff. A heap of warm cotton sheets from the dryer lies on the floor beside it.

c5.title: Pressing for a wedding party in Port Antonio
c5.text: A villa in Port Antonio sends ten cotton shirts, a black cotton dress and a polyester blouse to be ironed before a wedding. Trainee Omar has to get everything ready within two hours. The iron is set on hot. He takes a call and leaves the iron face down on a shirt for a moment.

c6.title: A complaint and a soiled bed in Treasure Beach
c6.text: On the day she checks out of a guest house in Treasure Beach, Mrs. Beverley Walters says that a blue blouse is missing from her returned laundry. The housekeeper, Janet, checks the list and finds that the blouse was written on it. Earlier the same day, Janet strips the bed of another room where a guest had been sick during the night.

questions.q: What should Shanice do about the socks that are not on the list?
o: Note them on the list as found, and tell the supervisor
Wash them with the shirts, as they came in the guest's bag
Put them back in the guest's room without telling anyone
Add them to the list and charge them with the other items
questions.why: An item that is not on the list may belong to someone else. Note it on the list and tell the supervisor, so it is agreed before it is washed or charged.

questions.q: What should Shanice do with the J$300 and the paper from the shorts pocket?
o: Put the money in the staff tip box and bin the paper
Record both and return them as the property's rules say
Read the paper, then call the number on it for the guest
Leave them in the pocket and wash the shorts as they are
questions.why: Anything in a pocket is the guest's property. Record it, keep it safe and return it as the rules say; never keep it, read private papers or wash it.

questions.q: How should the missing button be dealt with?
o: Sew on a new button so the shirt looks tidy when it is returned
Wash the shirt and say nothing, as buttons often come off in the wash
Note it on the list before washing, so the damage is on record
Take the button off the other shirt so the pair look the same
questions.why: Damage found before washing is written on the list so the guest cannot say the laundry caused it. Do not repair or change things without the guest's permission.

questions.q: Alecia finds a sorrel stain on the white napkin. What should she do before the napkin joins the white sheets in the machine?
o: Pre-treat it with a cotton-safe product, after a hidden-spot test
Wash it at once with the sheets, as the hot wash will take the colour out
Put it in the dryer first, as the heat will help to lift the red from the cloth
Press it with a hot iron, so the red dye dries out before it is washed
questions.why: Stains are pre-treated, with a hidden-spot test, before washing, and heat from a dryer or iron would set the red. The napkin is white cotton, so after treatment it can be washed with the white sheets.

questions.q: What does the hand in the washtub on the cardigan label mean?
o: It must be hand washed only
It can be machine washed on a wool cycle
It must be washed by hand and tumble dried
It must be hand washed with bleach
questions.why: A hand in the tub means hand wash only. It cannot go in the machine, and wool must never be tumble dried or washed hot.

questions.q: What does a crossed circle inside a square mean?
o: The item must be dry cleaned
The item must not be ironed
The item must be dried flat
The item must not be tumble dried
questions.why: A square with a circle is tumble drying; the cross means it must not be tumble dried. The iron symbol is for ironing and a plain circle is for dry cleaning.

questions.q: How should the lace blouse be washed?
o: In a mesh wash bag on a gentle cycle, or by hand if the label says so
In the hottest wash with the white sheets, as lace needs strong cleaning
Loose in a full machine so the other items protect it
With chlorine bleach to keep the lace bright
questions.why: Lace is delicate. A mesh bag stops it stretching and tangling, and a gentle wash keeps it from damage; hot water and bleach would spoil it.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do before using the new stain remover on the cream linen shirt?
o: Spray it on the front and see what happens, since it is only a shirt
Soak the shirt in it for an hour, so that it works well
Test it on a hidden part of the shirt and read the label
Mix it with bleach to make it stronger on the jerk sauce
questions.why: Test any stain remover on a hidden spot first, as some remove colour or harm the fabric. Never mix products.

questions.q: Dwayne wants to dry the towels, but the sunscreen marks are still visible after the wash. What should he do?
o: Treat and wash the towels again before drying them
Tumble dry them hot, as heat lifts the stain out
Iron them dry, to burn the sunscreen off
Fold them damp and tell the guest the marks are normal
questions.why: Heat sets a stain, so an item with a visible stain must not be dried. Treat it again and rewash; if it will not come out, tell the supervisor.

questions.q: Dwayne is unsure about the unknown stain on the white T-shirt. What is the best first step?
o: Rub hard with hot water until it fades
Read the label, then try a mild treatment on a hidden part first
Soak it in strong chlorine bleach for an hour
Put it through a hot tumble dry to see if it goes
questions.why: Check the label and test a gentle treatment on a hidden part. Rubbing hard damages fibres, bleach may harm the fabric, and drying sets the stain.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the dryer is slow and very hot?
o: The sheets are too wet for any dryer to dry
The detergent is making the drum heat up too much
The drum is too small for any sheets to dry in
The lint filter is blocked, so air cannot flow through
questions.why: Lint blocks the airflow, so drying takes longer and the dryer overheats. Cleaning the filter after every load prevents this fire risk.

questions.q: What should Natalie do first?
o: Switch it off, report it and clean the filter when safe
Add more sheets so the heat is used well
Open the door at once and pour water inside to cool it
Leave it running and clean the filter at the end of the shift
questions.why: A very hot dryer with a blocked filter is a fire risk. Switch it off, tell the supervisor and clean the filter once it is safe; never use water on a hot machine.

questions.q: In what order should Omar iron the items?
o: The black dress, then the shirts, then the polyester blouse
The shirts, then the polyester blouse, then the black dress
The polyester blouse first, then the cotton shirts and the dress
The shirts first, as there are most of them, then the other items
questions.why: Start with the lowest heat (the polyester blouse), then the hot cotton items. The iron cools slowly, so working from cool to hot saves time and prevents damage.

questions.q: How should Omar iron the black cotton dress to avoid shine?
o: On the right side with a very hot iron, pressing hard
Inside out, with the heat the label allows
On the right side, with the iron held still on each fold
Dry on the right side, with no cloth, to avoid water marks
questions.why: Ironing dark fabric directly on the right side can leave shiny marks. Press it inside out or through a pressing cloth, at the heat on the label.

questions.q: What went wrong when Omar left the iron face down on the shirt?
o: The shirt will be damp when he comes back
The iron may cool down and need to heat up again
The shirt may be scorched, and it is a fire risk
The steam will be wasted and the water tank will empty
questions.why: A hot iron left face down can scorch or burn the fabric and start a fire. Stand it upright or switch off and unplug it whenever you leave it.

questions.q: What should Janet do first about Mrs. Walters's missing blouse?
o: Tell her it must be in her room and to look again
Offer her money for a new blouse straight away
Check the list, search the laundry and tell the supervisor
Say that the blouse was never sent to the laundry
questions.why: Check your records and search, then report to the supervisor, who decides the response. Do not blame the guest or promise to pay.

questions.q: How should Janet handle the sheets from the room where a guest was sick?
o: Shake them out first to air the smell before bagging them
Put them in the normal linen bag and wash them with other sheets
Rinse them in the guest's bathroom basin to save time
Wear gloves, roll them up and bag them for the special wash
questions.why: Body fluids carry germs. Wear gloves, roll the sheets in on themselves, carry them away from your body, bag them as the property's rule says and wash your hands.

questions.q: A laundry list shows 5 shirts at J$450 each and 2 dresses at J$800 each, with an express charge of J$500. What is the total before tax?
questions.why: 5 shirts at J$450 is J$2,250; 2 dresses at J$800 is J$1,600; that is J$3,850, plus the J$500 express charge, makes J$4,350.

questions.q: A hotel keeps 3 sets of linen for every bed. What does this par level cover?
o: Three sheets that are put on each bed every day
One set in use, one in the wash and one clean on the shelf
Three washes that each sheet may have before it is thrown out
Three workers who must count the linen together
questions.why: A par level of 3 means three sets for each bed: one in use, one being washed and one ready on the shelf, so the room is never short.

questions.q: A care label shows an iron with one dot. What heat should you use?
o: Cool
Hot
Hot with steam
Medium-hot
questions.why: One dot is a cool iron, about 110 °C, used on synthetics. Two dots is warm and three dots is hot, used on cotton and linen.
